courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

examines Western theories of political authority, freedom, equality and pluralism that frame German debates about the state, citizenship and national identity
develops comparative analysis of democratic institutions, parties, backsliding and political participation for studying Germany in European comparison
introduces sociological concepts and theories for analysing institutions, identity, inequality, migration and social change
studies international-relations theories, geopolitics and multilateral negotiation as a framework for Germany’s role in Europe and the international order
develops qualitative research design, interviewing and interpretation of situated meanings for research on identity, migration and cultural debate
uses major literary works across historical periods to analyse community, authority, identity and cultural memory
studies empire, great-power politics and competing explanations of imperial rise and decline, supporting historical analysis of Germany and Europe
examines modernity, imperialism, colonial responses and major sociological debates that shape European social thought
directly studies European Union institutions, political authority, interests, legitimacy and policy making
studies film history, form and political context as cultural expression and provides methods for analysing German-language media without claiming German proficiency
develops archival and primary-source historical research through a Napoleonic European case involving German, Dutch, French, British and Polish actors
examines conflict causation, identity-based violence, reconciliation and peacebuilding in regional, national and international settings
traces warfare and military institutions in Western history from antiquity to the present, including the European conflicts central to modern German history
develops evidence-based analysis of misinformation, fake news, cognitive bias and scientific credibility for the evidenced political-culture and public-debate direction
studies civil society, social trust, public spheres, migrant inclusion and civil repair through contemporary sociological theory
analyses framing, persuasion, ethics and institutional communication in politics, law, media and public organisations
develops advanced analysis of literary-to-film adaptation, narration, image, music and sound as forms of cultural expression
studies how film, photography and music reproduce or resist racial power and how media connect identity, memory and political resistance
studies social movements and environmental justice, supporting the evidenced interest in environmental debates and civic mobilisation
examines how poetry, performance, voice and experimental media produce culturally situated meaning through critical and creative work
applies humanist, feminist, Marxist, minority and psychoanalytic perspectives in an advanced text-research project
analyses documentary representation across historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts and develops multimodal production
establishes practical criticism, genre analysis and literary interpretation for the evidenced literature direction
studies rhetoric, textual analysis, argument and oral presentation as ways language shapes public meaning
provides the brain, behaviour and research-method foundation required for advanced psycholinguistic study
uses stylistics and literary linguistics to analyse how phonetic, grammatical and discoursal choices create meaning in texts
compares literary and oral traditions, cultural transmission and representations of power across languages and regions
analyses how material media and technologies shape communication, knowledge circulation and cultural memory
analyses memoir, autobiography, diary and travel narratives as culturally situated accounts of identity and encounter
examines identity, conformity, marginalisation and social change through twentieth- and twenty-first-century popular media narratives
applies public speaking, debate and storytelling in a multilingual community setting, supporting intercultural communication without claiming German-language acquisition

alternatives.label: Modern Europe, politics & social change
alternatives.concept: Study modern European history, political institutions, international relations, migration, civil society, identity, conflict, environmental movements and public culture as a related social-science and humanities route. Use Germany as an evidenced motivating case while preserving the absence of German-language proficiency and a cumulative Germany-specific curriculum.
alternatives.labelReason: The label describes the completed curriculum’s modern European history, politics, sociology, conflict, media and public-culture content without presenting it as German Studies or German-language training.
progression: The schedule contains 24 unique courses / 180 EC, four courses per semester, Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and ten level-300 courses. Every course is available in its assigned Fall-2026-start term and none has a formal prerequisite. Introductory history, politics and sociology precede advanced EU politics, archival research, conflict, social theory, persuasion, literary-film and media analysis. No German-language prerequisite or proficiency is implied.

alternatives.label: Literature, media & cultural identity
alternatives.concept: Study how literary, rhetorical, linguistic and media forms create cultural meaning and express identity and power, combining textual interpretation, psycholinguistics, intercultural communication, film and multimodal production. Preserve German-language acquisition, German linguistics and Germany-specific cultural depth as explicit gaps.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed route concentrates on literature, stylistics, rhetoric, psycholinguistics, film, media and cultural identity; it does not claim German proficiency or a German Studies curriculum.
progression: The schedule contains 24 unique courses / 180 EC, four courses per semester, Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and eight level-300 courses. Every course is available in its assigned Fall-2026-start term; Introduction to Brain & Behavior precedes Psycholinguistics by four semesters. Introductory literature, rhetoric, sociology and film/media precede advanced persuasive, creative, interpretive and documentary work. No German-language competence is implied.
alternatives.distinctness: Ten courses / 75 EC differ in each direction. Comparative politics, international relations, modern sociology, EU politics, historical research, peace and conflict, Western military history, misinformation and environmental movements are replaced by literary studies, rhetoric, psycholinguistics, media archaeology, life writing and community communication. The change shifts the programme from modern European institutions and social change to language, literature and mediated cultural identity.

candidates.label: German proficiency, German linguistics and German-language writing

selection.assessment: Two complete related-field programmes pass the evidence, course-content, schedule and pairwise 30-EC distinctness gates. A third German-proficiency, German-linguistics and German-language-writing route is not feasible because the current UCR workbook contains no German-language course, cumulative proficiency sequence, German grammar or German-language academic writing. Psycholinguistics and stylistics contribute genuine language study but cannot be expanded into or labelled as German proficiency.

blocks: Both study language acquisition and analysis; UCR provides general psycholinguistics rather than contrastive German linguistics or German-language proficiency.
Both analyse how language and literary form create meaning; UCR uses English-language stylistics rather than German acquisition through German literature.
Both connect narrative form with human experience; UCR is general creative communication rather than German-language acquisition through health and narrative.
UCR has no German-language acquisition sequence corresponding to the first proficiency course.
UCR has no German-language acquisition through German film or an equivalent second proficiency course.
Both develop interpretation of literature and culture across historical contexts; UCR is general literary studies rather than German culture before 1945.
Both apply critical perspectives to culture and representations of nature; UCR is cross-cultural literary theory rather than German cultural criticism.
Both study modern cultural expression through media and film; UCR is general film and media history rather than German culture after 1945.
Both examine technology as a cultural object; UCR studies material media histories rather than machines and algorithms in German literature.
Both examine identity, conformity, marginalisation and social change through cultural narratives; UCR uses mainly American media rather than German migration and minorities.
Both analyse how cultural expression represents identity, difference and power; UCR centres race and media rather than gender and diversity in German culture.
Both examine misinformation and public reasoning; UCR is a general critical-information course rather than German political culture and populism.
Both situate regions within wider historical and political structures; UCR studies empires globally rather than providing German regional studies.
Both examine political authority, national identity and territorial order; UCR provides general political philosophy rather than the comparator’s Germany-focused philosophy course.
Both examine European integration, political institutions and Germany’s European setting; UCR studies EU politics comparatively rather than from a specifically German perspective.
Both introduce humanities and social-science approaches to understanding societies; UCR is a sociology foundation rather than the comparator’s integrated humanities course.
UCR’s selected social-science route has no dedicated course on the Rhineland economic model in Germany and Europe.
The compulsory 30-EC Germany Studies semester abroad remains separate and is not replaced by scheduled UCR courses.
The genuine 30-EC profiling space remains open and is not equated with scheduled UCR courses.
The compulsory Germany Studies thesis remains separate; UCR optional independent research is comparison-only and not scheduled degree credit.

notes.text: The UCR alternatives study modern European history and politics, migration, civil society, conflict, literature, media, rhetoric, psycholinguistics and cultural identity. UCR does not offer German proficiency progression, German linguistics, German-language academic work, a cumulative Germany-specific cultural sequence or the required semester abroad, so these are related humanities and social-science routes rather than German Language and Culture equivalents.
